newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania to announce reform package next week.
newsitem.headline: Romania to announce reform package next week.

text.p: Romania will set forth a tough reform package early next week, following loan talks with international lenders, the government said on Thursday.
A government statement said Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea would announce reforms of the economy, coupled with social protection steps, during a news conference late next Monday.

IMF and World Bank negotiators have been working with the government for more than one month on the reforms, including faster restructuring and privatisation of industries, as well as price and currency markets liberalisation.
Bucharest is seeking up to $1.0 billion in total loans from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank needed to push through with its reform drive.
Both lenders had withheld credits to Romania last year over foreign exchange market curbs and overspending by the former ruling leftists in an election year.
Romania is struggling with rising inflation and bulging deficits. Confidence is sagging in the local leu currency, which has lost 68 percent against the dollar in the New Year.
Ciorbea's centrist coalition government, which came in after last November's elections, is facing mounting pressure from trade unions over pay demands to cushion price rises.
Labour leaders are seeking assurances regarding safety nets against looming unemployment as the government moves ahead with plans to streamline loss-making communist-era industries.
Romanians, whose purchasing power was halved in the post-communist era, now earn some $60 in average monthly wages.

Local analysts say that the outcome of last November's vote -- when ex-communists were removed from office for the first time in seven years -- reflects many Romanians' weariness with the country's slow and painful transition to the free market.
Year-on-year inflation hit 56.9 percent in 1996 -- more than triple the target agreed with the Fund.
Inflation is forecast to soar to 97.0 percent this year, led by January's fuel price rises and further plans to liberalise electricity and food price.
The 1996 state budget gap is believed to have widened to 5.7 percent of gross domestic product, from a forecast of 2.2 percent. -- Bucharest Newsroom, 40-1 3120264
